units.unitTitle: Rocks, Soils and the Rock Cycle
units.unitOverview: The ground under your feet is not one material. It is rock of three different families, each made in a different way, with soil on top of it that came from the rock itself. This unit teaches you to tell the three families apart, shows how a fossil survives inside one of them, looks at what soil is actually made of, and then puts the whole thing in motion: rock is not permanent, and the same material has been used and reused for billions of years.
sources: Cambridge Primary Science Teacher's Resource 6, topics on rocks, soils and the rock cycle
outcomes: Name the three families of rock and say how each one forms.
Identify a rock's family from features you can see.
Explain how a fossil forms, and why it is found in only one of the three families.
Describe what soil is made of and how it forms from rock.
Classify a soil by its clay, sand and organic content.
Explain how soil composition affects what will grow in it.
Describe the rock cycle and name the processes that move material round it.

concepts.title: Three Families of Rock
concepts.explanation:
Every rock on Earth belongs to one of three families, and which family it is depends entirely on HOW IT WAS MADE rather than on what it is made of.

IGNEOUS rock forms when molten rock cools and hardens. The word comes from the Latin for fire. If it cools slowly deep underground the crystals grow large and you can see them easily, which is granite. If it cools fast at the surface after a volcanic eruption the crystals have no time to grow and the rock looks almost smooth, which is basalt - the rock most of the Rift Valley's lava flows are made of. The tell for an igneous rock is interlocking crystals with no layers at all.

SEDIMENTARY rock forms from sediment: loose grains of sand, mud and broken shell carried by water and dropped in layers, usually on a seabed or riverbed. Over a very long time the layers are buried, squeezed and cemented into solid rock. Sandstone and limestone are sedimentary. The tell is LAYERS, and often grains you can see or rub off, and sometimes fossils.

METAMORPHIC rock is either of the other two changed by enormous heat and pressure without melting. The word means 'changed in form'. Limestone under pressure becomes marble; mudstone becomes slate, which splits into flat sheets and is why slate makes roof tiles. The tell is crystals like an igneous rock but arranged in bands or stripes, as though the rock has been squeezed in one direction.

So the three questions to ask a rock are: does it have layers, does it have interlocking crystals, and are those crystals banded.
concepts.example: Three samples on a desk. One is speckled with big grey and pink crystals and has no layers - granite, igneous, cooled slowly underground. One is pale, gritty and clearly striped in bands you could count - sandstone, sedimentary. One is dark, hard and splits into flat sheets - slate, metamorphic, once mud.

concepts.title: How a Fossil Survives
concepts.explanation:
A FOSSIL is the preserved remains or trace of a living thing from long ago, turned to stone inside a rock. Almost every fossil ever found is in SEDIMENTARY rock, and the reason is worth working out rather than remembering.

The usual sequence runs like this. An animal or plant dies and its body settles somewhere sediment is being laid down - a riverbed, a lakebed, the sea floor. The soft parts rot away quickly, so what is usually left is bone, shell or wood. More sediment settles on top, layer on layer, burying it deeper. Over a very long time, water carrying dissolved minerals seeps through, and those minerals slowly replace the original material, particle by particle, until what remains has the shape of the bone and the substance of rock. Later, the rock above may be worn away and the fossil is exposed at the surface, which is how they are found.

Now the reason it has to be sedimentary. An igneous rock was molten - nothing living survives being melted. A metamorphic rock has been through such heat and pressure that any fossil in it is crushed and destroyed. Only sedimentary rock forms gently enough, at low temperature, and by burying things, which is exactly what a fossil needs.

A fossil is not the animal. It is rock in the animal's shape, which is why a fossil bone is far heavier than a real one and cannot be broken and eaten by anything.

And fossils are almost always very old - millions of years, not hundreds - because the burying, the mineral replacement and the wearing away above all take a very long time.
concepts.example: A fossil shell is found part-way up a hillside far inland. Three things follow: the rock is sedimentary, that place was once under water, and the whole hillside was later lifted up - because the shell certainly did not climb.

concepts.title: What Soil Is Actually Made Of
concepts.explanation:
Soil looks like one brown substance and is in fact a mixture of four things, and the proportions decide almost everything about it.

The largest part is MINERAL GRAINS, and these came from rock. Rain, frost, roots and moving water break rock down into smaller and smaller pieces over a very long time - that is WEATHERING - and those pieces are the grit and dust in soil. The grains come in three sizes and the names matter: SAND grains are the largest and you can feel them as grit; SILT is finer; CLAY grains are the smallest of all and feel smooth and sticky when wet.

The second part is ORGANIC MATTER, also called humus: the dark, crumbly remains of dead leaves, roots and animals, broken down by the decomposers you met in the ecosystems unit. It is what makes good soil dark, and it holds both water and nutrients.

The third and fourth are AIR and WATER, in the gaps between the grains. Roots need both, which is why a soil packed hard with no gaps grows very little.

So a soil is classified by which grain size dominates and how much organic matter it holds. A SANDY soil is mostly large grains, so water runs straight through it - it drains well, dries fast and loses its nutrients quickly. A CLAY soil is mostly the finest grains, so the gaps are tiny: it holds water so well that it waterlogs, and it sets hard when dry. A LOAM is a mixture of all three sizes with plenty of organic matter, and it is what a farmer hopes for, because it holds enough water without drowning the roots.
concepts.example: Rub a pinch of damp soil between your finger and thumb. If it feels gritty and falls apart, it is sandy. If it smears smooth and you can roll it into a thread, it has a great deal of clay. If it feels slightly gritty, holds together and smells earthy, it is a loam - and the dark colour is the organic matter.

concepts.title: Why the Soil Decides the Crop
concepts.explanation:
Soil composition is not a detail. It decides what will grow, how much water a field needs, and whether a harvest fails - and it can be changed, which is why any of this is worth knowing.

A plant needs three things from its soil: water, nutrients, and air around its roots. Each soil type supplies these differently. SANDY soil has large gaps, so water drains away fast and carries dissolved nutrients with it; it is easy to dig and warms early, and it dries out and goes hungry. CLAY soil holds water and nutrients well and holds them too well: the gaps are so small that water fills them all and the roots have no air, which drowns them, and in dry weather it bakes into a hard crust seedlings cannot push through. LOAM does both jobs adequately, which is why it grows most things.

And composition changes, in both directions. It gets WORSE when heavy rain washes the fine particles and nutrients away, when the same crop is grown year after year and takes the same nutrients out each time, or when the soil is left bare and the wind removes the top layer - the richest one. It gets BETTER when organic matter is put back: compost, manure or the remains of a previous crop dug in. Organic matter helps both problem soils, and it is the same substance either way - it opens up a clay soil so air and water can move, and it binds a sandy one so it holds water instead of losing it.

So the farmer's question is never just 'is this good soil'. It is 'what is this soil short of, and what would put it back'.
concepts.example: Two fields of maize a kilometre apart get the same rain. One is on sandy soil and the plants are short and yellowing, because the nutrients washed through weeks ago. The other has had manure dug in for years and the maize is tall and dark green. Same rain, same seed, different soil - and the difference was made, not found.

concepts.title: The Rock Cycle
concepts.explanation:
The three rock families are not three separate things that happen once. Each one can become either of the others, over and over, and the whole set of routes is called the ROCK CYCLE. Once you can see it as a cycle, rock stops being permanent.

Start with molten rock. It COOLS and SOLIDIFIES into igneous rock - fast at the surface, slowly underground.

Exposed at the surface, any rock is attacked. WEATHERING breaks it into loose grains; EROSION carries those grains away in rivers, wind and ice. They are TRANSPORTED and then DEPOSITED in layers somewhere lower down, usually under water. Buried, squeezed and cemented - COMPACTION and CEMENTATION - the layers become sedimentary rock.

Bury any rock deep enough and it meets great HEAT AND PRESSURE, which changes it without melting it into metamorphic rock.

Bury it deeper or hotter still and it MELTS, becoming molten rock again - and the cycle closes.

Every step can be skipped or repeated. A sedimentary rock can be weathered straight back into sediment without ever becoming metamorphic. An igneous rock can be metamorphosed and then melted. There is no fixed order and no starting point, which is why it is drawn as a circle with arrows both ways.

The time involved is the hardest part to hold. A single trip round takes many millions of years, and the atoms in a pebble you pick up today have very probably been through it several times, in rocks that no longer exist.
concepts.example: A grain of sand on a beach was once part of a granite mountain. Weathering freed it, a river carried it to the sea, and it will be buried and cemented into sandstone. If that sandstone is later pushed deep under a mountain range it will become quartzite, and if it goes deeper still it will melt - and one day cool as granite again.

explorations.title: Which Family Is This Rock?
explorations.context: To classify rocks by observable features rather than by guessing from colour.
explorations.prompt: Collect six different stones. For each, answer three questions in writing: does it have layers, does it have interlocking crystals, are the crystals in bands? Then name its family and say which feature decided it.
explorations.answer: Layers mean sedimentary; interlocking crystals with no layers mean igneous; crystals in bands or stripes mean metamorphic. Colour decides nothing - granite comes in several colours and so does sandstone.
explorations.hint: Wet each stone and look at it in good light. Layers and crystals both show up far better damp than dry.
explorations.explanation: Three Families of Rock: which family a rock belongs to is decided by how it formed, and each way of forming leaves a different visible mark.

explorations.title: What Is in This Soil?
explorations.context: To separate a soil sample into its parts and judge its composition.
explorations.prompt: Half-fill a clear jar with soil, top it up with water, screw the lid on and shake hard. Stand it somewhere still for a day, then describe the layers from the bottom up and estimate the share of each.
explorations.answer: Sand settles first at the bottom, then silt, then clay on top, with organic matter floating and water above. The thickness of each band gives you the soil's composition, and a thick clay band explains poor drainage.
explorations.hint: Leave it a full day - the clay is so fine that it is still settling hours later, and a reading taken too early makes the soil look sandier than it is.
explorations.explanation: What Soil Is Actually Made Of: soil is a mixture of mineral grains of three sizes, organic matter, air and water, and the proportions decide how it behaves.

explorations.title: Which Soil Holds Water?
explorations.context: To measure how differently two soils drain, and link it to what would grow in them.
explorations.prompt: Put equal amounts of sandy soil and clay soil in two funnels lined with filter paper. Pour the same amount of water through each and measure what comes out the bottom in two minutes. Predict first.
explorations.answer: Far more water runs straight through the sandy soil, because its gaps are large. The clay soil holds most of it back, which is why clay waterlogs and sand dries out.
explorations.hint: Pack both soils to the same firmness, or you will be testing your packing instead of the soil.
explorations.explanation: Why the Soil Decides the Crop: grain size sets the gap size, gap size sets the drainage, and drainage decides whether roots get water or drown.

methods.title: Classifying a Rock
methods.example: To decide which of the three families a rock belongs to, using what you can see.
steps: Wet the rock and look at it in good light.
Ask: can you see layers or bands of different material? If yes, it is sedimentary.
If not, ask: can you see crystals locked together? If yes, it is igneous or metamorphic.
Ask: are those crystals lined up in stripes? Stripes mean metamorphic; no pattern means igneous.
Try rubbing it: if grains come off on your fingers, that is more evidence for sedimentary.
Write down which feature decided your answer, not just the answer.

methods.title: The Jar Test for Soil
methods.example: To find the proportions of sand, silt and clay in a soil sample.
steps: Half-fill a straight-sided clear jar with soil and top it up with water.
Seal it and shake hard for a full minute, until no lumps remain.
Stand it somewhere it will not be knocked and leave it for 24 hours.
Measure the depth of each band: sand at the bottom, then silt, then clay.
Work out each band as a share of the total, and name the soil type.
Note any floating material - that is the organic matter.

methods.title: Tracing a Route Round the Rock Cycle
methods.example: To describe how one rock could become another, naming every process on the way.
steps: Write down the rock you are starting with and its family.
Write down the rock you are ending with and its family.
List the processes needed, in order, from weathering, erosion, transport, deposition, compaction, cementation, heat and pressure, melting, cooling and solidifying.
Check each step actually leads to the next - you cannot cement something that has not been deposited.
Say roughly how long the route would take, and where on Earth each step happens.

workedExamples.title: Naming a rock from its look
workedExamples.prompt: A rock is pale, feels gritty, and has clear horizontal stripes of slightly different colours. Which family, and how do you know?
workedExamples.solution: Sedimentary. The stripes are layers of sediment laid down one after another, and the grittiness is the individual grains. Neither igneous nor metamorphic rock is made of loose grains you can feel, and igneous rock has no layers at all.

workedExamples.title: Why no fossils in granite
workedExamples.prompt: Explain why a fossil is never found in granite.
workedExamples.solution: Granite is igneous, which means it formed from molten rock. Nothing living survives being melted, so there is nothing left to preserve. Fossils need a rock that forms gently and by burying things, and that is sedimentary rock - laid down cold, in layers, on a riverbed or seabed.

workedExamples.title: Advising a farmer with clay soil
workedExamples.prompt: A farmer's field waterlogs in the rains and bakes hard in the dry season. What is the soil, and what would you advise?
workedExamples.solution: It is a clay soil: the grains are so fine that the gaps are tiny, which holds water in the rains and sets solid when dry. Digging in organic matter - compost, manure or crop remains - opens the soil so air and water can move through it. The same addition would help a sandy soil, for the opposite reason: there it binds the soil so it holds water instead of losing it.

workedExamples.title: From mountain to sandstone and back
workedExamples.prompt: Describe how granite in a mountain could become granite again, naming every process.
workedExamples.solution: Weathering breaks the granite into grains; erosion and transport carry them down a river; deposition lays them in layers on a seabed; compaction and cementation make sandstone. Buried deeper, heat and pressure turn it into quartzite - metamorphic. Deeper or hotter still it melts, and cooling and solidifying make it igneous granite once more. Many millions of years for one lap.

practice.prompt: Name the three families of rock.
practice.answer: Igneous, sedimentary and metamorphic.
practice.hint: One is made by fire, one by layers, one by change.

practice.prompt: How does igneous rock form?
practice.answer: Molten rock cools and solidifies - fast at the surface, slowly underground.
practice.hint: The name comes from the Latin for fire.

practice.prompt: What visible feature tells you a rock is sedimentary?
practice.answer: Layers, and often grains you can see or feel.
practice.hint: It was laid down a bit at a time.

practice.prompt: In which family of rock are fossils found, and why only that one?
practice.answer: Sedimentary. It forms gently, at low temperature, by burying things - igneous rock was molten and metamorphic rock has been crushed by heat and pressure, and neither leaves a fossil intact.
practice.hint: Ask what would happen to a bone in each of the three processes.

practice.prompt: Name the four things soil is made of.
practice.answer: Mineral grains from weathered rock, organic matter (humus), air and water.
practice.hint: Two of them are in the gaps rather than being solid.

practice.prompt: Put sand, silt and clay in order from largest grain to smallest.
practice.answer: Sand, then silt, then clay.
practice.hint: The one you can feel as grit is the biggest.

practice.prompt: Why does water run straight through a sandy soil?
practice.answer: Its grains are large, so the gaps between them are large and water passes through easily - carrying dissolved nutrients with it.
practice.hint: Big grains, big gaps.

practice.prompt: Digging in compost helps both a clay soil and a sandy one. Explain how one substance helps two opposite problems.
practice.answer: Organic matter opens a clay soil so air and water can move through it, and binds a sandy soil so it holds water instead of losing it. It improves the structure either way.
practice.hint: The two soils have opposite faults, and both faults are about the size of the gaps.

practice.prompt: Name the processes that turn loose sediment into sedimentary rock.
practice.answer: Deposition lays it down in layers, then compaction squeezes it and cementation glues the grains together.
practice.hint: Three words, in that order.

practice.prompt: A fossil sea shell is found high up a hill far from the sea. What three things does that tell you?
practice.answer: The rock is sedimentary, that place was once under water, and the land has since been lifted up.
practice.hint: The shell did not travel there by itself.

activities.title: The rock family sort
activities.materials: Six or more different stones from around where you live, water, and a bright light.
steps: Wet each stone and look at it carefully in good light.
For each, write yes or no to: layers? interlocking crystals? crystals in bands?
Use your three answers to name the family, and write down which answer decided it.
Put any stone you could not decide about in a separate pile and say what made it hard.

activities.title: The soil jar
activities.materials: A straight-sided clear jar with a lid, a trowel of soil, water, a ruler.
steps: Half-fill the jar with soil, top up with water, seal and shake hard for a minute.
Stand it somewhere still and leave it a full day.
Measure the depth of each band from the bottom and work out each as a share of the total.
Name your soil type, and say one crop that would do well in it and one that would struggle.

activities.title: Draw the cycle and walk a route
activities.materials: A large sheet of paper and coloured pencils.
steps: Draw the three rock families in a triangle, with molten rock in the middle.
Draw and label an arrow for every process that leads from one to another.
Trace one complete route with your finger and say each process aloud in order.
Now trace a DIFFERENT route between the same two rocks, to show there is no fixed order.

rules.text: A rock's family is decided by HOW it formed, not by its colour.
Fossils are found almost only in sedimentary rock, because the other two destroy them.
Grain size sets gap size, gap size sets drainage.
Any rock can become any other. The rock cycle has no starting point and no fixed order.

terms: Rock formed when molten rock cooled and solidified.
Rock formed from layers of sediment, compacted and cemented.
Rock changed by great heat and pressure without melting.
The preserved remains or trace of a living thing, turned to stone.
The breaking down of rock in place, by rain, frost, roots and heat.
The carrying away of broken rock by water, wind or ice.
The laying down of transported sediment in layers.
The squeezing of buried sediment by the weight above it.
The gluing together of sediment grains by dissolved minerals.
The dark crumbly organic matter in soil, from decayed plants and animals.
The smallest mineral grains in soil; smooth, sticky, and holds water.
The largest mineral grains in soil; gritty, and drains fast.
A soil mixing sand, silt and clay with plenty of organic matter.
The set of routes by which any rock family can become any other.
commonMistakes: A rock's family can be told from its colour.
It cannot. Granite comes in grey, pink and near-black, and so does sandstone. Layers, crystals and banding are the features that decide it.
Fossils can be found in any rock.
Almost only in sedimentary rock. Igneous rock was molten and metamorphic rock has been crushed, and neither leaves a fossil intact.
A fossil IS the bone.
It is rock in the bone's shape. The original material was replaced, particle by particle, by minerals carried in water.
Soil is just crushed rock.
Mineral grains are the largest part, and soil is also organic matter, air and water - and it is the organic matter that makes it fertile.
Rocks last forever.
Every rock is on its way to becoming another one. A single lap of the rock cycle takes millions of years, which is why it looks permanent.

connections.text: Digging in manure changes a soil's structure, which changes what it will grow - the science is the reason it works.
Slate roofs exist because a metamorphic rock splits into flat sheets, and granite kerbs because an igneous rock is hard and has no layers to split along.
The dark basalt of the lava flows is igneous rock that cooled fast at the surface, which is why its crystals are too small to see.
The jar test turns 'this soil feels heavy' into three numbers you can compare with somebody else's field.

realProblems.context: A gardener's vegetable bed floods after every rain and the seedlings rot.
realProblems.prompt: What is the likely soil type, and what would you advise?
realProblems.answer: A clay soil - the grains are so fine that water fills every gap and the roots get no air. Digging in plenty of organic matter would open the structure so water can drain and air can reach the roots.
realProblems.hint: Rotting roots is a sign of too little air, not too little water.
realProblems.errorFeedback: Clay holds water too well; organic matter dug in opens the gaps so the bed can drain.

realProblems.context: A builder digging a foundation finds a layer of rock full of shell fossils, with hard crystalline rock beneath it.
realProblems.prompt: What can you say about each layer, and which is older?
realProblems.answer: The fossil layer is sedimentary and was laid down under water. The crystalline layer below has no fossils and is igneous or metamorphic. The lower layer is older, because sediment is laid down on top of what is already there.
realProblems.hint: In undisturbed layers, deeper means older.
realProblems.errorFeedback: Fossils mean sedimentary and water; the crystalline rock beneath is older, because layers pile up from the bottom.

realProblems.context: Someone argues that quarrying is harmless because 'the rock will just grow back'.
realProblems.prompt: Use the rock cycle to answer them properly - what is right and what is wrong in that claim?
realProblems.answer: The cycle is real, so the material is not destroyed and will eventually become rock again. What is wrong is the timescale: one lap takes many millions of years, so nothing grows back on any human scale. The material is recycled; the rock, the hillside and the habitat are not replaced.
realProblems.hint: Agree with the part that is true before correcting the part that is not.
realProblems.errorFeedback: The cycle does recycle the material, over millions of years - which is far too slow to replace a quarried hillside in any useful sense.

reasoningPrompts.prompt: Explain why fossils are found in sedimentary rock and almost never in the other two families.
keyIdeas: Sedimentary rock forms gently, by burying
Igneous rock was molten
Metamorphic rock has been crushed by heat and pressure
reasoningPrompts.modelAnswer: A fossil needs its remains buried gently and left undisturbed, and that is exactly how sedimentary rock forms: sediment settles in layers over the body, cold, and slowly cements around it. Igneous rock formed from molten rock, and nothing living survives melting. Metamorphic rock has been through such heat and pressure that any fossil in it is crushed out of shape. Only one of the three processes is gentle enough.

reasoningPrompts.prompt: Organic matter improves both clay soil and sandy soil, although their problems are opposite. Explain how.
keyIdeas: Clay has gaps too small, sand too large
Organic matter changes the structure
It opens clay and binds sand
reasoningPrompts.modelAnswer: The two soils fail in opposite directions and for the same underlying reason - the size of the gaps between their grains. Clay's gaps are so small that water fills them all and roots get no air; sand's are so large that water runs straight through and takes the nutrients with it. Organic matter changes the structure rather than the grains: it opens a clay soil so water and air can move, and it binds a sandy one so it holds water. One substance, two opposite faults, because both faults are about structure.

reasoningPrompts.prompt: Why is the rock cycle drawn as a circle with arrows both ways, rather than as a list of stages in order?
keyIdeas: Any family can become any other
Steps can be skipped or repeated
There is no starting point
reasoningPrompts.modelAnswer: Because there is no fixed order. A sedimentary rock can be weathered straight back into sediment without ever becoming metamorphic; an igneous rock can be changed by pressure and then melted; the same material can go round several times. A list would imply a beginning and an end, and the cycle has neither - which is the whole point, because it means the rock under your feet is made of material that has been something else before.

questions.question: Igneous rock forms when:
options: heat and pressure change a rock
questions.hint: The name comes from the Latin for fire.
questions.explanation: Igneous rock forms from molten rock - slowly underground makes large crystals, quickly at the surface makes small ones.

questions.question: A rock with clear layers is most likely:
questions.hint: Layers are laid down one at a time.
questions.explanation: Sediment settles in layers, so layering is the mark of sedimentary rock. Igneous rock has none.

questions.question: Which is the SMALLEST of these soil grains?
questions.hint: It feels smooth and sticky rather than gritty.
questions.explanation: Clay grains are the finest, which is why clay soils hold water and set hard when dry.

questions.question: The dark crumbly organic matter in soil is called:
questions.hint: It comes from decayed plants and animals.
questions.explanation: Humus is decayed organic matter. It makes soil dark and holds both water and nutrients.

questions.question: Fossils are almost never found in igneous rock because:
options: the rock was molten, so nothing living survived
questions.answer: the rock was molten, so nothing living survived
questions.hint: Ask what happens to a bone at melting temperature.
questions.explanation: Igneous rock formed from molten rock, and nothing living survives that. Fossils need the gentle burying that makes sedimentary rock.

questions.question: Water drains quickly through sandy soil because:
options: its large grains leave large gaps
it contains no clay at all
questions.answer: its large grains leave large gaps
questions.hint: Grain size sets gap size.
questions.explanation: Large grains leave large gaps, so water passes through easily - taking dissolved nutrients with it.

questions.question: Slate splits into flat sheets because it is:
questions.hint: It was once mud, and something happened to it.
questions.explanation: Slate is mudstone changed by heat and pressure. The squeezing lined up its crystals, which is why it splits into sheets - and why it makes roof tiles.

questions.question: Which process carries broken rock away from where it formed?
questions.hint: One of these breaks rock in place; the other moves it.
questions.explanation: Weathering breaks rock down where it stands; erosion is the carrying away by water, wind or ice.

questions.question: In a soil jar test left for a day, the bands from the bottom up are:
questions.hint: The heaviest grains reach the bottom first.
questions.explanation: The largest and heaviest grains settle first, so sand is at the bottom and the finest clay is on top - with organic matter floating above.

questions.question: A fossil shell is found high on an inland hill. Which conclusion is best supported?
options: that place was once under water and has since been lifted
the shell was carried there by a bird
the fossil formed in the air
questions.answer: that place was once under water and has since been lifted
questions.hint: Where does the rock that holds fossils form?
questions.explanation: Fossil-bearing rock is sedimentary and forms under water, so the site was submerged. Finding it high up means the land has risen since.

units.unitOverview: The Earth is one of eight planets going round one star, with a moon of its own going round it. This unit puts those motions in order, explains why the Moon appears to change shape when it never does, and shows how both facts come from the same cause: things in space moving in paths set by gravity.
sources: Cambridge Primary Science Teacher's Resource 6, topics on the Solar System and the Moon
outcomes: Name the eight planets in order from the Sun.
Describe the relative positions of the Sun, the planets and the Moon.
Explain what orbits what, and what holds each orbit in place.
Describe the Moon's phases over a month.
Explain why the Moon appears to change shape when it does not.
Tell the difference between a star, a planet and a moon.

concepts.title: The Solar System, in Order
concepts.explanation:
At the centre of the Solar System is the SUN, and the first thing to be clear about is what it is: a STAR, one of countless billions, and the only object in the Solar System that makes its own light. Everything else we see out there is shining with light borrowed from it.

Eight PLANETS orbit the Sun. In order outwards: Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars, Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus, Neptune. The first four are small and rocky; the outer four are enormous and made mostly of gas and ice. Between Mars and Jupiter is a belt of rocky rubble called asteroids.

The distances are the part worth dwelling on, because diagrams cannot show them honestly. If the Sun were the size of a football, the Earth would be a grain of sand about 25 metres away, and Neptune would be another grain three quarters of a kilometre off. Almost all of the Solar System is empty space.

A MOON is an object that orbits a planet rather than the Sun. The Earth has one; Jupiter has more than ninety. So there is a clear ladder: moons orbit planets, planets orbit the Sun, and the Sun is a star.

What holds it all together is GRAVITY. The Sun is so massive that its gravity reaches out past Neptune and keeps every planet curving round it instead of flying off in a straight line. The Earth's own gravity does the same job for the Moon, on a much smaller scale.

The farther out a planet is, the longer its year, because it has further to travel and moves more slowly. Mercury goes round in 88 days; Earth takes 365; Neptune takes about 165 Earth years.
concepts.example: Look at the night sky and you can see two quite different kinds of point. The stars twinkle and stay in fixed patterns night after night. The planets - Venus and Jupiter are the brightest - shine steadily and slowly change position against the stars from week to week, which is how the word 'planet', meaning wanderer, was earned.

concepts.title: What Goes Round What
concepts.explanation:
Three motions are happening at once, and confusing them is the commonest difficulty in this whole subject. Take them one at a time.

The Earth SPINS on its own axis, once in 24 hours. That gives day and night: the side facing the Sun is lit and the side facing away is dark, and every place passes through both as it turns. Nothing about the Sun moving is involved - the Sun appears to cross the sky because we are the ones rotating.

The Earth ORBITS the Sun, once in about 365 days. That is a year, and it is a much slower motion, going on all the time underneath the daily spin.

The MOON orbits the Earth, once in about 27 days, while being carried round the Sun along with us.

So the Moon goes round the Earth, the Earth goes round the Sun, and the Earth spins all the while. Three motions, three different periods, all at once.

The tell for whether you have it straight is this question: does the Sun go round the Earth? It does not, and it never has - but it certainly looks as if it does, and for most of human history that was the sensible conclusion from the available evidence. What settled it was careful records of where the planets appear night after night, which only make sense if the Earth is one of the things going round.

One more point worth fixing. The Moon keeps the same face towards us always, because it turns once on its own axis in exactly the time it takes to go round us. There is no permanently dark side - the far side gets just as much sunlight; we simply never see it.
concepts.example: Stand a lamp on a table for the Sun, hold a ball for the Earth and walk slowly round the lamp while spinning the ball. Every spin is a day. One lap is a year. Now have someone circle a smaller ball round yours as you walk - that is the Moon, doing its own lap while being carried round the lamp with you.

concepts.title: Why the Moon Seems to Change Shape
concepts.explanation:
Watch the Moon for a month and it appears to change shape completely: a thin crescent, then half, then a full bright circle, then shrinking back and vanishing. It does none of this. The Moon is a ball, always, and it is always exactly half lit by the Sun - the same as the Earth is. What changes is how much of that lit half we can see from here.

The Moon has no light of its own. It shines with reflected sunlight, which is why the lit part always faces the Sun.

As the Moon goes round us, our viewing angle changes. When it is roughly between us and the Sun, its lit half faces away and we see almost nothing - a NEW MOON. A week later we are looking at it side-on and see exactly half of the lit half, which appears as a half circle - the FIRST QUARTER. A week after that the Moon is on the far side from the Sun, its whole lit half faces us, and we see a FULL MOON. Another week gives the LAST QUARTER, and then it thins back to new.

The whole cycle takes about 29 and a half days, which is where a month comes from.

The usual mistake is to think the phases are the Earth's shadow falling on the Moon. They are not - that is an eclipse, which is a rare event, and phases happen every month without fail. The phases are simply geometry: a half-lit ball, seen from changing angles.

Waxing means the lit part is growing; waning means it is shrinking.
concepts.example: Hold a ball at arm's length in a dark room with a single lamp to one side. Turn slowly on the spot, keeping the ball in front of you, and watch it: a crescent, then half, then fully lit, then back. The ball never changed and the lamp never moved. Only your angle did.

concepts.title: Star, Planet, Moon
concepts.explanation:
Three words that get used loosely, and the differences are precise and worth having.

A STAR makes its own light, by reactions in its core, and is enormous. The Sun is a star, and an ordinary one - it looks special only because it is close. Every other star you can see is far enough away to be a point of light however much you magnify it.

A PLANET makes no light of its own. It is a large object orbiting a star, shining only by reflecting that star's light, and it is round because its own gravity pulled it into a ball. There are eight in our Solar System.

A MOON is a natural object orbiting a PLANET. It also makes no light of its own. Our Moon is one; Jupiter has more than ninety, some of them larger than Mercury.

So the difference between a planet and a moon is not size but what it goes round. And the difference between a star and the other two is whether it makes its own light.

There is one more word worth adding. A SATELLITE is anything that orbits something larger, so our Moon is a natural satellite of the Earth - and the spacecraft we launch are artificial ones, doing the same job by design: relaying telephone calls, photographing weather systems, and showing farmers where rain has fallen.

A quick test: if it makes its own light it is a star; if it does not and goes round a star it is a planet; if it does not and goes round a planet it is a moon.
concepts.example: On a clear night, the brightest object after the Moon is often Venus - and it is a planet, reflecting sunlight, not a star. It gives itself away by not twinkling, and by having moved against the star patterns when you look again a fortnight later.

explorations.title: Making the Phases with a Ball
explorations.context: To show that the Moon's phases come from the viewing angle and not from any change in the Moon.
explorations.prompt: In a darkened room, put one lamp on a table. Hold a pale ball at arm's length and turn slowly on the spot, keeping the ball in front of you. Draw what the ball looks like at four points a quarter turn apart.
explorations.answer: The ball appears as a crescent, then half lit, then fully lit, then half the other way - the Moon's phases exactly. The ball never changed shape and the lamp never moved.
explorations.hint: Keep the ball at the same height and the same distance the whole way round, or you will be changing two things at once.
explorations.explanation: Why the Moon Seems to Change Shape: the Moon is always a half-lit ball, and the phases are how much of the lit half happens to face us.

explorations.title: A Month of Moon Watching
explorations.context: To record the Moon's phases over time and find the length of the cycle from your own data.
explorations.prompt: Every clear evening for four weeks, sketch the Moon's shape and write the date. Then work out how many days passed between one full moon and the next.
explorations.answer: About 29 and a half days from full moon to full moon. The shape changes in a repeating, predictable cycle - and the record proves it in a way that remembering cannot.
explorations.hint: Sketch it even on the nights it looks the same as yesterday - the gaps in a record are what make the count wrong.
explorations.explanation: Why the Moon Seems to Change Shape: the cycle takes about 29 and a half days, which is where the month came from.

explorations.title: The Solar System to Scale
explorations.context: To find out how misleading every picture of the Solar System is about distance.
explorations.prompt: Take a football as the Sun. A grain of sand 25 m away is the Earth. Work out where Neptune would be, then pace it out if you have the room.
explorations.answer: Neptune would be about 750 m away - three quarters of a kilometre from the football. Almost all of the Solar System is empty space, which no diagram that fits on a page can show.
explorations.hint: Neptune is about thirty times as far from the Sun as the Earth is, so multiply your 25 m by thirty.
explorations.explanation: The Solar System, in Order: the planets orbit at distances so large that any diagram showing them all on one page must shrink the gaps enormously.

methods.title: Is It a Star, a Planet or a Moon?
methods.example: To classify an object in the sky from what it does rather than how bright it looks.
steps: Ask whether it makes its own light. If it does, it is a star.
If it does not, ask what it orbits.
Orbiting a star makes it a planet; orbiting a planet makes it a moon.
Check with two observations: a star twinkles and holds its place in a pattern; a planet shines steadily and shifts against the stars over weeks.
Write down which observation decided it.

methods.title: Explaining a Phase
methods.example: To say why the Moon looks the way it does tonight.
steps: Draw the Sun, the Earth and the Moon in a line or at a right angle as tonight requires.
Shade the half of the Moon that faces away from the Sun - that half is always dark.
Mark where you are on the Earth and look along your line of sight to the Moon.
Work out how much of the LIT half you can see from there.
Name the phase, and say whether it is waxing or waning.

methods.title: Keeping Three Motions Apart
methods.example: To describe what causes day, a year and a month without confusing them.
steps: Name the motion: is it a spin on an axis, or an orbit round something?
Say what is moving and what it is moving around.
Give its period - 24 hours, 27 days, 365 days.
Say what we observe because of it - day and night, the Moon's phases, the seasons.
Check you have not made the Sun move: it does not go round us, however it looks.

workedExamples.title: Naming the planets in order
workedExamples.prompt: List the eight planets from the Sun outwards, and say which are rocky.
workedExamples.solution: Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars, Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus, Neptune. The first four - Mercury, Venus, Earth and Mars - are the small rocky ones. The outer four are giants made mostly of gas and ice, with a belt of asteroids between Mars and Jupiter.

workedExamples.title: Why day and night are not caused by the Sun moving
workedExamples.prompt: The Sun appears to cross the sky each day. Explain what is actually happening.
workedExamples.solution: The Earth is spinning on its axis, once in 24 hours. The side facing the Sun is in daylight and the side facing away is in darkness, and every place passes through both as the Earth turns. The Sun is not moving across the sky; we are rotating past it, which produces exactly the same appearance.

workedExamples.title: Why a full moon happens
workedExamples.prompt: Explain the positions of the Sun, Earth and Moon at full moon.
workedExamples.solution: At full moon the Earth is roughly between the Sun and the Moon. The Sun lights the half of the Moon facing it, and because that is also the half facing us, we see the whole lit circle. Two weeks later the Moon is on the other side, its lit half faces away from us, and we see almost nothing - a new moon.

workedExamples.title: Phases are not eclipses
workedExamples.prompt: A friend says the phases happen because the Earth's shadow falls on the Moon. Explain why that cannot be right.
workedExamples.solution: If the phases were the Earth's shadow they would happen only when the three bodies lined up exactly, which is rare - that IS an eclipse, and eclipses happen a few times a year. Phases happen every single month, without fail, and pass through the whole cycle. They are caused by our changing view of a permanently half-lit ball, not by any shadow.

practice.prompt: What is at the centre of the Solar System, and what kind of object is it?
practice.answer: The Sun, which is a star - the only object in the Solar System that makes its own light.
practice.hint: Everything else shines with borrowed light.

practice.prompt: Name the eight planets in order from the Sun.
practice.answer: Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars, Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus, Neptune.
practice.hint: Four small rocky ones, then four giants.

practice.prompt: How long does the Earth take to spin once, and what does that give us?
practice.answer: 24 hours, which gives day and night.
practice.hint: It is the fastest of the three motions in this unit.

practice.prompt: What does the Moon orbit, and how long does it take?
practice.answer: The Earth, in about 27 days - while being carried round the Sun with us.
practice.hint: It is not going round the Sun on its own.

practice.prompt: What holds the planets in their orbits?
practice.answer: The Sun's gravity. It is so massive that its pull reaches past Neptune and keeps each planet curving round instead of flying off straight.
practice.hint: The same force that makes a dropped mango fall.

practice.prompt: Why does the Moon shine?
practice.answer: It reflects sunlight. It makes no light of its own.
practice.hint: Only one object in the Solar System makes its own light.

practice.prompt: How long is the Moon's full cycle of phases?
practice.answer: About 29 and a half days, which is where the month comes from.
practice.hint: Count from one full moon to the next.

practice.prompt: Explain the difference between a planet and a moon.
practice.answer: It is what they orbit, not their size. A planet orbits a star; a moon orbits a planet. Some moons are bigger than some planets.
practice.hint: Ask what it goes round.

practice.prompt: Why is it wrong to say the phases are caused by the Earth's shadow?
practice.answer: That describes an eclipse, which is rare and needs an exact line-up. Phases happen every month and come from our changing view of a Moon that is always half lit by the Sun.
practice.hint: How often do phases happen, and how often do eclipses?

practice.prompt: Why does Neptune take about 165 Earth years to go round the Sun?
practice.answer: It is about thirty times as far out as the Earth, so its path is enormously longer, and it also travels more slowly the further from the Sun it is.
practice.hint: Two reasons, and both add to the time.

activities.title: Three motions with three people
activities.materials: A lamp or torch, a large ball, a small ball, and a dark room.
steps: Stand the lamp in the middle as the Sun. One person holds the large ball as the Earth and spins it slowly while walking round the lamp.
A second person carries the small ball round the Earth as it walks.
Count one spin as a day, one lap of the lamp as a year, one lap of the Earth as a month.
Swap places so everyone has seen it from each position, and write down which motion was hardest to keep track of.

activities.title: A month of Moon sketches
activities.materials: A notebook, a pencil, and four weeks of clear evenings.
steps: Sketch the Moon's shape each evening and write the date beside it.
Mark every night you could not see it, and why - cloud, or it had not risen.
After four weeks, count the days from one full moon to the next.
Write down how close your figure came to 29 and a half days, and what would have made it more accurate.

activities.title: Pacing out the Solar System
activities.materials: A football, a few grains of sand, a long measuring tape or a known pace length, and a large open space.
steps: Put the football down as the Sun.
Pace out 25 metres and put a grain of sand there for the Earth.
Work out and pace out where Mars, Jupiter and Neptune would be, if you have room.
Write one sentence about what every textbook picture of the Solar System has to leave out.

rules.text: Moons orbit planets, planets orbit the Sun, and the Sun is a star.
Only a star makes its own light. Planets and moons shine by reflection.
The Moon is always half lit. The phases are how much of the lit half faces us.
Phases happen every month; eclipses are rare. They are not the same thing.

terms: An object that makes its own light. The Sun is one.
A large object orbiting a star, shining only by reflected light.
A natural object orbiting a planet.
Anything orbiting something larger - natural, like the Moon, or artificial.
The curved path one object takes around another.
The imaginary line a planet spins around.
The Sun and everything held in orbit by its gravity.
A rocky object, smaller than a planet, most of them between Mars and Jupiter.
The shape of the lit part of the Moon as seen from Earth.
The phase when the lit half faces away and we see almost nothing.
The phase when the whole lit half faces us.
When the lit part we can see is growing.
When the lit part we can see is shrinking.
commonMistakes: The Sun goes round the Earth.
The Earth spins, which makes the Sun appear to cross the sky. The Earth orbits the Sun, and not the other way round - it took careful records of the planets to settle it.
The Moon changes shape.
It is always a ball and always half lit. What changes is how much of the lit half we can see from where we are.
The phases are the Earth's shadow on the Moon.
That is an eclipse, and eclipses are rare. Phases happen every month, which alone shows they cannot be caused by an exact line-up.
The Moon has a permanently dark side.
The far side gets just as much sunlight. We never see it because the Moon turns once on its axis in exactly the time it takes to orbit us.
The Moon makes its own light.
Only stars do. The Moon reflects sunlight, which is why the lit part always faces the Sun.

connections.text: A month began as the Moon's cycle of phases, which is why it is about 29 or 30 days and not a round number.
Tides follow the Moon, so anyone launching a boat is using the Moon's position whether they name it or not.
A weather forecast and a map both arrive by artificial satellite - an object put into orbit to do deliberately what the Moon does naturally.
A month of sketches is a record, and a record settles an argument that memory cannot.

realProblems.context: Someone points at a very bright steady light in the evening sky and calls it the brightest star.
realProblems.prompt: How would you find out whether it is a star or a planet?
realProblems.answer: Look at whether it twinkles - stars do, planets shine steadily - and note its position against the star patterns, then check again a fortnight later. If it has moved against them it is a planet. It is very likely Venus.
realProblems.hint: One test works tonight; the better one needs two weeks.
realProblems.errorFeedback: A steady light that shifts against the star patterns over weeks is a planet, and Venus is the usual answer.

realProblems.context: A child says the Moon was broken last week because only a thin sliver of it was there.
realProblems.prompt: Explain what was really happening, in a way a younger child could follow.
realProblems.answer: The Moon is always a whole ball and the Sun always lights one half of it. Last week we were looking at it from an angle where almost all the lit half was turned away, so only a thin sliver showed. Nothing broke, and in two weeks the whole lit side will face us.
realProblems.hint: Use the ball and lamp - it is easier to show than to say.
realProblems.errorFeedback: The Moon is always a half-lit ball; the sliver was how much of the lit half faced us from here.

realProblems.context: A textbook diagram shows all eight planets neatly spaced across one page.
realProblems.prompt: What is the diagram right about and what is it badly wrong about, and why can it not do both?
realProblems.answer: It is right about the order and about everything orbiting the Sun. It is badly wrong about distance and size - on a true scale, if the Sun were a football the Earth would be a grain of sand 25 m away and Neptune 750 m off. It cannot do both, because a page that showed the distances truly would leave the planets invisibly small.
realProblems.hint: Ask what would have to shrink for the whole system to fit on a page.
realProblems.errorFeedback: The order is right, the distances are hugely compressed, and no single page can show both honestly.

reasoningPrompts.prompt: Explain why the Moon appears to change shape during a month, when it never does.
keyIdeas: The Moon is always a half-lit ball
Our viewing angle changes as it orbits
The phases are how much of the lit half faces us
reasoningPrompts.modelAnswer: The Moon is a ball and the Sun always lights exactly half of it, just as it lights half the Earth. As the Moon travels round us our angle on that lit half changes, so we see different amounts of it - almost none at new moon, half of it a week later, all of it at full moon. The Moon itself does not change at all; only our view of it does.

reasoningPrompts.prompt: People once believed the Sun travels round the Earth. Explain why that was reasonable, and what settled it.
keyIdeas: It is exactly what the sky looks like
Records of the planets gave new evidence
The spin explains the same appearance
reasoningPrompts.modelAnswer: It is precisely what you see: the Sun rises on one side and sets on the other every day without fail, and with only your eyes that is the sensible conclusion. What settled it was careful records of where the planets appear night after night, whose looping paths only make sense if the Earth is one of the things going round the Sun. The Earth's own spin produces the same daily appearance, which is why the old idea fitted the evidence available at the time.

reasoningPrompts.prompt: Some moons are larger than some planets. Explain how that can be true without the words losing their meaning.
keyIdeas: The difference is what it orbits, not how big it is
A planet orbits a star
A moon orbits a planet
reasoningPrompts.modelAnswer: The words describe what an object goes round, not how large it is. A planet orbits a star; a moon orbits a planet. Jupiter's largest moons are bigger than Mercury, and they are still moons because they circle Jupiter rather than the Sun. If size decided it the categories would be useless, because there is no size that separates them.

questions.question: The Sun is:
questions.hint: It is the only thing in the Solar System making its own light.
questions.explanation: The Sun is an ordinary star. It looks special only because it is so much closer than all the others.

questions.question: Which planet is third from the Sun?
questions.hint: Mercury, Venus, then us.
questions.explanation: The order outwards is Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars, then the four giants.

questions.question: The Moon orbits:
questions.hint: A moon goes round a planet.
questions.explanation: The Moon orbits the Earth in about 27 days, while being carried round the Sun along with us.

questions.question: The Moon shines because it:
questions.hint: Only stars make their own light.
questions.explanation: The Moon has no light of its own, which is why the lit part always faces the Sun.

questions.question: Day and night are caused by:
options: the Earth spinning on its axis
the Sun going round the Earth
the Earth's orbit of the Sun
questions.answer: the Earth spinning on its axis
questions.hint: Which motion takes 24 hours?
questions.explanation: The Earth turns once in 24 hours, so every place passes through the lit side and the dark side. The Sun does not move across the sky; we rotate past it.

questions.question: What holds the planets in orbit around the Sun?
questions.hint: The Sun's mass is enormous.
questions.explanation: The Sun is so massive that its gravity reaches past Neptune, keeping each planet curving round instead of flying off in a straight line.

questions.question: The Moon's full cycle of phases takes about:
questions.hint: It is where the month came from.
questions.explanation: One full moon to the next is about 29 and a half days, which is why a month is roughly that length.

questions.question: At full moon, the Earth is:
options: roughly between the Sun and the Moon
questions.answer: roughly between the Sun and the Moon
questions.hint: We must be able to see the whole lit half.
questions.explanation: With the Earth between them, the Moon's sunlit half faces us and we see the complete circle.

questions.question: Why can the phases NOT be the Earth's shadow on the Moon?
options: phases happen every month, but exact line-ups are rare
the Moon is too far away
the Moon makes its own light
questions.answer: phases happen every month, but exact line-ups are rare
questions.hint: Compare how often phases happen with how often eclipses do.
questions.explanation: A shadow needs an exact line-up, which is an eclipse and happens a few times a year. Phases run their full cycle every month, so they must have another cause - our changing view.

questions.question: What makes something a moon rather than a planet?
options: it orbits a planet rather than a star
questions.answer: it orbits a planet rather than a star
questions.hint: Some moons are bigger than some planets.
questions.explanation: The words describe what an object goes round. Jupiter's largest moons beat Mercury for size and are still moons, because they circle Jupiter.

units.unitOverview: You already know that light travels in straight lines and bounces off surfaces. This unit takes both a step further: it shows exactly where a ray goes when it strikes a mirror, and what happens to it when it passes from air into water or glass. Two rules, both of which you can measure, and between them they explain mirrors, lenses, rainbows and why a straw in a glass looks broken.
sources: Cambridge Primary Science Teacher's Resource 6, topics on reflection and refraction
outcomes: Describe how a ray of light changes direction when it reflects from a plane mirror.
Measure the angle of incidence and the angle of reflection and compare them.
Use the law of reflection to predict where a reflected ray will go.
Describe what happens to a ray of light passing from one medium into another.
Name that change of direction as refraction and explain what causes it.
Explain everyday effects, such as a straw appearing bent, using refraction.

concepts.title: What a Ray Does at a Mirror
concepts.explanation:
A PLANE MIRROR is a flat mirror, and what a light ray does when it strikes one is precise enough to be a law.

First the words, because they have to be exact. The ray arriving is the INCIDENT ray; the ray leaving is the REFLECTED ray. Draw a line at right angles to the mirror at the point where the ray hits, and that line is the NORMAL. The ANGLE OF INCIDENCE is between the incident ray and the normal. The ANGLE OF REFLECTION is between the reflected ray and the normal. Note that both angles are measured from the NORMAL and not from the mirror's surface - measuring from the surface is the commonest error here, and it gives the wrong number every time even though the two angles still come out equal.

The LAW OF REFLECTION is then short: the angle of incidence equals the angle of reflection. Shine a ray in at 30 degrees to the normal and it leaves at 30 degrees on the other side. At 50 it leaves at 50. Straight at the mirror - zero degrees - and it comes straight back along its own path.

Because the law is exact, reflection is predictable, and that is what makes mirrors useful rather than merely shiny. You can work out before you start where a ray will go, which is how a periscope is designed, how a dentist's mirror is angled, and how a driver's mirror is set to show the road behind.

Why a mirror and not a wall? Both reflect light. A mirror's surface is so smooth that all the rays arriving together leave together, still in order, so the pattern survives and you see an image. A wall is rough at a small scale, so the rays scatter in every direction - you see the wall, and no image in it.
concepts.example: A ray box shines a beam onto a mirror on a sheet of paper. Mark the incident ray, the reflected ray and the normal, then measure both angles with a protractor: 34 and 34. Turn the mirror a little and measure again: 51 and 51. The two are equal every time, to within the degree a protractor can read.

concepts.title: Light Changes Direction Between Materials
concepts.explanation:
Light travels in straight lines - through one material. Send it from one material into another and it changes direction at the boundary, and that change is called REFRACTION.

The material light travels through is called a MEDIUM: air, water and glass are the three that matter here. Light moves fastest in air, more slowly in water, and slower still in glass. That difference in speed is the whole cause of refraction, and it is worth stating plainly, because 'light bends' sounds like magic until you know why.

A useful picture: imagine a line of people walking in step across a field and entering deep mud at an angle. The first person to reach the mud slows down while the others are still on grass, so the whole line pivots. Light does the same thing at the boundary, for the same reason.

The direction of the bend follows a rule. Going from a faster medium into a slower one - air into water or glass - the ray bends TOWARDS the normal. Going the other way, from slower to faster, it bends AWAY from the normal. And a ray arriving exactly along the normal, straight on, does not bend at all, because there is no side to slow down first.

So two different things can happen to a ray at a boundary, and they are worth keeping apart. At a mirror it bounces back and the angles are equal - reflection. At the surface of water or glass it passes through and changes direction - refraction. At a window you get both at once, which is why you can see the street and faintly see yourself.
concepts.example: Shine a narrow beam at an angle into a tank of water. You can see the beam kink sharply at the surface, bending towards the normal as it enters. Aim it straight down instead and it goes through without bending at all - the same water, the same light, and no bend, because nothing entered first.

concepts.title: What Refraction Explains
concepts.explanation:
Refraction is not a laboratory curiosity. Once you can see it, a set of everyday puzzles all turn out to be the same thing.

A STRAW IN A GLASS OF WATER looks bent or broken at the surface. It is perfectly straight. Light from the underwater part of the straw bends as it leaves the water and enters the air, so it reaches your eye from a slightly different direction than it started - and your brain, which assumes light travels in straight lines, places that part of the straw where the light appears to have come from.

A COIN AT THE BOTTOM OF A BUCKET looks nearer the surface than it is, and water is always shallower to look at than to step into. The same bending, and the same assumption by the brain, is why.

A FISH seen from the bank is not quite where it appears, which anyone who has tried to spear one learns quickly.

A LENS is refraction put to work on purpose. A curved piece of glass bends every ray that enters it by a controlled amount, so all the rays from one point can be brought back together at another point. That is the whole principle of a magnifying glass, a camera, a pair of spectacles and the lens inside your own eye.

And a RAINBOW is refraction plus one extra fact: the different colours in white light bend by slightly different amounts. Each raindrop refracts the sunlight entering it, reflects it off the inside of the back of the drop, and refracts it again on the way out - and because the colours bend differently, they leave separated.
concepts.example: Put a coin in an opaque cup and step back until the rim just hides it. Keep still while someone pours water in, and the coin comes into view without anything moving. The light from it is now bending as it leaves the water, arriving at your eye from a direction it could not have taken before.

concepts.title: Two Rules, Side by Side
concepts.explanation:
This unit has two laws, and the useful thing is to be able to say which one applies before you start drawing.

REFLECTION happens when light meets a surface it cannot pass through, and comes back. The rule is that the angle of incidence equals the angle of reflection, both measured from the normal. The medium does not change, because the light never enters the mirror.

REFRACTION happens when light passes from one transparent medium INTO another, and continues on a new course. The rule is about direction: into a slower medium it bends towards the normal, into a faster one away from it, and straight along the normal it does not bend at all. The medium does change, which is the entire cause.

So the question to ask is whether the light passed through the boundary or came back off it. Passed through means refraction; came back means reflection.

Most real surfaces do both. A window reflects a little and transmits most, which is why shop glass shows you a faint version of yourself over the display. Water does both too - a lake reflects the sky and you can also see the stones on the bottom, and which one dominates depends on the angle you are looking from. Standing right over it you see the stones; looking across it from low down you see the sky.

And one thing neither rule permits: light does not turn corners on its own. Both laws describe what happens AT a boundary. In between, in a single medium, light travels in straight lines, which is why you cannot see round a wall and why shadows have edges.
concepts.example: Look into a still pool from directly above and you see the bottom, because most of the light is refracting up out of the water to your eye. Crouch down and look across the same pool at a shallow angle and you see the sky and the trees instead - most of the light now reflecting off the surface. Same water, two rules, and the angle decides.

explorations.title: Measuring the Two Angles
explorations.context: To test the law of reflection by measuring, rather than taking it on trust.
explorations.prompt: Stand a mirror upright on paper and shine a narrow beam at it. Mark the incident ray, the reflected ray and the normal. Measure both angles with a protractor. Repeat at five different angles.
explorations.answer: The angle of incidence and the angle of reflection are equal at every setting, to within a degree or two - which is the reading error of a protractor, not a real difference.
explorations.hint: Draw the normal FIRST, at right angles to the mirror where the beam hits. Measuring from the mirror's surface instead is the mistake that spoils this experiment.
explorations.explanation: What a Ray Does at a Mirror: the law of reflection says the two angles are equal, both measured from the normal - which is what makes a mirror predictable.

explorations.title: Watching a Beam Bend
explorations.context: To see refraction happen and find out when it does not.
explorations.prompt: Shine a narrow beam into a tank of water at a steep angle, then a shallow one, then straight down. Sketch the path each time and describe when the bend is largest and when there is none.
explorations.answer: The beam bends towards the normal on entering the water, and the bend is largest at the shallowest angle. Aimed straight along the normal there is no bend at all.
explorations.hint: A little milk or chalk dust in the water makes the beam visible all the way through instead of only where it enters.
explorations.explanation: Light Changes Direction Between Materials: refraction happens because light travels at different speeds in different media, and a ray arriving straight on has no side to slow first.

explorations.title: The Coin That Reappears
explorations.context: To use refraction to explain something that looks impossible.
explorations.prompt: Put a coin in an opaque cup and step back until the rim just hides it. Stay completely still while someone slowly pours water in. Describe what happens and explain it with a ray diagram.
explorations.answer: The coin comes into view without anyone moving. Light from it now refracts as it leaves the water, arriving at your eye from a direction it could not have travelled before.
explorations.hint: You must not move at all, or you will have changed the one thing the experiment depends on.
explorations.explanation: What Refraction Explains: your brain assumes light travelled in a straight line, so it places the coin where the light appears to have come from.

methods.title: Drawing a Reflected Ray
methods.example: To predict where a ray will go after it hits a plane mirror.
steps: Draw the mirror as a straight line and mark where the ray strikes it.
Draw the normal: a dashed line at right angles to the mirror at that point.
Measure the angle between the incident ray and the normal.
Draw the reflected ray on the other side of the normal at exactly the same angle.
Label both angles and mark them equal.
Check: both angles measured from the NORMAL, never from the mirror.

methods.title: Drawing a Refracted Ray
methods.example: To show what happens to a ray passing from air into water or glass.
steps: Draw the boundary as a straight line and mark where the ray meets it.
Draw the normal at right angles to the boundary at that point.
Decide which way the ray is going: into a slower medium, or out into a faster one.
Into a slower medium, draw the ray continuing but bent TOWARDS the normal; out into a faster one, bend it AWAY.
If the ray arrives along the normal, draw it straight through with no bend.
Label the media on each side, since the bend depends entirely on which is which.

methods.title: Explaining an Everyday Effect
methods.example: To account for something that looks wrong, using reflection or refraction.
steps: Say whether the light passed through a boundary or bounced off it - that chooses your rule.
Identify the two media, if it passed through.
Sketch the real path of the light from the object to the eye, with the bend at the boundary.
Now sketch the straight line the eye ASSUMES the light came along.
Where those two lines disagree is where the object appears to be, and that is your explanation.

workedExamples.title: A ray at 40 degrees
workedExamples.prompt: A ray strikes a plane mirror at 40 degrees to the normal. At what angle does it leave, and in which direction?
workedExamples.solution: At 40 degrees to the normal, on the opposite side of the normal from the incident ray. The law of reflection says the angle of incidence equals the angle of reflection, so 40 in means 40 out - and the ray leaves on the other side of the normal, not back along the same side.

workedExamples.title: Why a wall has no reflection in it
workedExamples.prompt: A mirror and a white wall both reflect light. Why can you see your face in only one of them?
workedExamples.solution: A mirror's surface is smooth enough that rays arriving together leave together, keeping their arrangement, so the pattern of light from your face survives and forms an image. A wall is rough at a very small scale, so each ray leaves in its own direction and the pattern is scattered. Both reflect; only one preserves the image.

workedExamples.title: The broken straw
workedExamples.prompt: Explain why a straight straw looks bent where it enters a glass of water.
workedExamples.solution: The straw is straight. Light from the underwater part bends as it leaves the water and enters the air, so it reaches your eye from a different direction than it set off in. Your brain assumes light travels in straight lines and places that part of the straw along the line the light arrived on - which is not where it actually is. The result is a visible kink exactly at the water's surface, where the bending happens.

workedExamples.title: A ray that does not bend
workedExamples.prompt: A ray enters a glass block and continues in a perfectly straight line. What can you conclude?
workedExamples.solution: That it arrived along the normal - straight on to the surface, at zero degrees. Refraction happens because one side of the beam enters the slower medium before the other and slows first, which pivots it. A ray arriving square to the surface has no side entering first, so there is nothing to pivot and it passes straight through, even though it does slow down.

practice.prompt: State the law of reflection.
practice.answer: The angle of incidence equals the angle of reflection.
practice.hint: Both are measured from the same line.

practice.prompt: What is the normal in a ray diagram?
practice.answer: A line drawn at right angles to the surface, at the point where the ray strikes it.
practice.hint: Both angles are measured from it.

practice.prompt: A ray hits a mirror at 25 degrees to the normal. At what angle does it leave?
practice.answer: 25 degrees, on the other side of the normal.
practice.hint: The law makes this a one-step answer.

practice.prompt: What is refraction?
practice.answer: The change of direction of light as it passes from one medium into another.
practice.hint: It happens at the boundary, not on the way through.

practice.prompt: Why does light refract at all?
practice.answer: Because it travels at different speeds in different media. One side of the beam enters the new medium first and changes speed first, which pivots the beam.
practice.hint: Think of a line of people walking into mud at an angle.

practice.prompt: Going from air into water, which way does a ray bend?
practice.answer: Towards the normal, because water is the slower medium.
practice.hint: Slower medium, towards; faster medium, away.

practice.prompt: When does a ray pass into water without bending at all?
practice.answer: When it arrives along the normal - straight on to the surface.
practice.hint: Nothing enters first, so there is nothing to pivot.

practice.prompt: Explain why a straw in water looks bent.
practice.answer: Light from the underwater part refracts as it leaves the water, so it reaches the eye from a different direction. The brain assumes light travelled in a straight line and places that part of the straw along the arriving line, which is not where it is.
practice.hint: The straw is fine. The explanation is about the light and the brain.

practice.prompt: How do you decide whether a situation is reflection or refraction?
practice.answer: Ask whether the light came back off the boundary or passed through it. Back off means reflection; through means refraction.
practice.hint: One question settles it.

practice.prompt: Looking straight down into a pool you see the bottom; looking across it you see the sky. Explain.
practice.answer: Both happen at once and the angle decides which dominates. From above, most light refracts up out of the water and you see the bottom. At a shallow angle, most reflects off the surface and you see the sky.
practice.hint: Real surfaces do both.

activities.title: The protractor test
activities.materials: A small flat mirror, paper, a pencil, a protractor, and a narrow beam of light or sunlight through a slit in card.
steps: Stand the mirror upright on the paper and draw a line along its base.
Shine the beam at the mirror and mark two points on the incoming beam and two on the outgoing one.
Take the mirror away and join the marks, then draw the normal where the rays meet.
Measure both angles and record them. Repeat at five different angles and write down whether the pairs matched.

activities.title: Bent straws and vanishing coins
activities.materials: A clear glass, a straw or straight stick, an opaque cup, a coin, water.
steps: Stand the straw in the empty glass and look at it from the side. Add water and look again.
Sketch what you see before and after, marking exactly where the kink appears.
Put the coin in the opaque cup and back away until the rim hides it, then have water poured in while you hold still.
Write one explanation that accounts for BOTH observations, using refraction.

activities.title: Which rule is this?
activities.materials: A notebook, and a walk around where you live.
steps: Find six situations involving light: a window, a puddle, a spoon in a cup, a mirror, a shiny pot, a pair of spectacles.
For each, write down whether the light came back off a boundary or passed through it.
Name the rule that applies, and say which observation told you.
Mark any situation where BOTH are happening, and say how you can tell.

rules.text: The angle of incidence equals the angle of reflection - both measured from the NORMAL.
Light refracts because it travels at different speeds in different media.
Into a slower medium a ray bends towards the normal; into a faster one, away from it.
A ray arriving along the normal does not bend at all.

terms: The ray of light arriving at a surface.
The ray of light leaving a surface after reflection.
A line at right angles to a surface at the point a ray strikes it.
The angle between the incident ray and the normal.
The angle between the reflected ray and the normal.
The angle of incidence equals the angle of reflection.
The change of direction of light passing from one medium into another.
The material light is travelling through - air, water or glass.
A curved piece of glass that refracts rays by a controlled amount.
The picture of an object formed by light, as in a mirror.
commonMistakes: The angles are measured from the mirror's surface.
They are measured from the NORMAL, the line at right angles to the surface. Measuring from the surface gives the wrong number every time, even though the two still come out equal.
Light bends because it 'wants' to.
It changes direction because it travels at a different speed in the new medium, and one side of the beam enters first. No speed change, no bend.
A straw in water is really bent.
It is perfectly straight. The light from its lower part bends on leaving the water, and the brain places the straw along the line the light arrived on.
Reflection and refraction are the same thing.
Reflection comes back off a boundary; refraction passes through it. A window does both at once, which is why you see the street and faintly yourself.
A rough wall does not reflect light.
It reflects it in all directions at once, which is why you can see the wall. A mirror is simply smooth enough to keep the rays in order, so an image survives.

connections.text: A driver's mirror is angled using the law of reflection: the angle it is set at decides exactly which piece of road comes into view.
A fish is never quite where it looks, because the light from it bends on leaving the water - which is why spearing one takes practice.
Every lens is refraction used on purpose, bending rays by a controlled amount so they meet again at one point.
A rainbow is refraction twice and reflection once inside every raindrop, with the colours separating because each bends by a slightly different amount.

realProblems.context: A shopkeeper wants a mirror high in the corner so that from the till she can see the doorway she cannot otherwise see.
realProblems.prompt: How would you work out the angle to fix it at?
realProblems.answer: Draw the light path from the doorway to the mirror to her eye.
