At the mirror, the incoming and outgoing rays must make equal angles with the normal, so the mirror has to be turned until its normal bisects the angle between those two directions. Fixing it by guesswork and adjusting is the same thing done slowly.
realProblems.hint: The mirror's normal must sit exactly halfway between the two directions.
realProblems.errorFeedback: Set the mirror so its normal bisects the angle between the line to the doorway and the line to her eye - that is the law of reflection applied.

realProblems.context: A child wading into a river says the water is much deeper than it looked from the bank.
realProblems.prompt: Explain why water always looks shallower than it is.
realProblems.answer: Light from the riverbed bends away from the normal as it leaves the water into the air, so it reaches the eye from a steeper direction than it set off. The brain assumes a straight path and places the bed higher up than it really is, making the water look shallower.
realProblems.hint: The bed appears wherever the arriving light SEEMS to have come from.
realProblems.errorFeedback: Refraction at the surface makes light from the bed arrive from a steeper direction, so the bed appears raised and the water looks shallower.

realProblems.context: Someone claims a shop window 'is a mirror at night and a window in the day', and that the glass must change.
realProblems.prompt: Correct them using both rules from this unit.
realProblems.answer: The glass does not change at all. It always reflects a little and transmits most. In daylight the light coming from the street is far brighter than the light inside, so what you mostly see is the transmitted view. At night the inside is brighter than the street, so the small reflected part is what dominates and you see yourself. Same glass, same two rules, different brightness on the two sides.
realProblems.hint: Ask what changed between day and night - the glass, or the light on each side of it?
realProblems.errorFeedback: The glass reflects a little and transmits most at all times; what changes is which side is brighter.

reasoningPrompts.prompt: Why must both angles in a reflection be measured from the normal rather than from the mirror?
keyIdeas: The normal is at right angles to the surface
It gives one fixed reference for both angles
Measuring from the surface gives a different number
reasoningPrompts.modelAnswer: The normal is a single fixed line at right angles to the surface, so both angles are measured against the same reference and can be fairly compared. Measuring from the mirror's surface gives the complementary angle instead - 60 where the true angle is 30 - and although the two still come out equal as each other, every number is wrong and any prediction made from them fails. It also stops working entirely for a curved mirror, where 'the surface' has no single direction.

reasoningPrompts.prompt: Explain why a ray entering water along the normal does not bend, when one entering at an angle does.
keyIdeas: Refraction is caused by a change of speed
At an angle, one side of the beam enters first
Along the normal, the whole beam enters together
reasoningPrompts.modelAnswer: Refraction happens because light travels more slowly in water, and at an angle one side of the beam reaches the water before the other. That side slows first while the rest is still in air, so the beam pivots - like a line of people walking into mud at an angle. A ray arriving straight along the normal has its whole width entering at the same instant, so nothing slows before anything else and there is nothing to pivot. The light still slows down; it simply carries straight on.

reasoningPrompts.prompt: Explain what the bent-straw illusion tells us about how seeing works.
keyIdeas: The brain assumes light travelled in a straight line
The light actually bent at the surface
We see objects where the light SEEMS to come from
reasoningPrompts.modelAnswer: The straw is straight and the illusion is in the seeing, not the straw. Light from the underwater part bends as it leaves the water, so it arrives at the eye along a different line than it set out on. The brain has no way of knowing that and works on the assumption light travels in straight lines, so it traces the arriving ray straight back and places that part of the straw along it. What this shows is that we do not see objects directly - we see where the light appears to have come from, and any bend on the way puts the object somewhere it is not.

questions.question: The law of reflection says the angle of incidence is:
options: equal to the angle of reflection
questions.answer: equal to the angle of reflection
questions.hint: It is the shortest law in this unit.
questions.explanation: The angle of incidence equals the angle of reflection, both measured from the normal.

questions.question: The normal is drawn:
options: at right angles to the surface
questions.answer: at right angles to the surface
questions.hint: It is the reference both angles are measured from.
questions.explanation: The normal is perpendicular to the surface at the point the ray strikes, and both angles are measured from it.

questions.question: Refraction is the change of direction of light when it:
options: passes from one medium into another
questions.answer: passes from one medium into another
questions.hint: It happens at a boundary the light goes THROUGH.
questions.explanation: Refraction happens when light crosses from one medium into another and changes speed.

questions.question: Light travels most slowly in:
questions.hint: Fastest in air, slower in water, slower still in glass.
questions.explanation: Light is fastest in air, slower in water and slowest in glass - and that difference is what causes refraction.

questions.question: A ray strikes a mirror at 35 degrees to the normal. It leaves at:
questions.hint: Apply the law directly.
questions.explanation: The angle of reflection equals the angle of incidence, so 35 in gives 35 out, on the other side of the normal.

questions.question: Passing from air into water, a ray bends:
questions.hint: Water is the slower medium.
questions.explanation: Entering a slower medium bends a ray towards the normal; leaving into a faster one bends it away.

questions.question: You can see your face in a mirror but not in a white wall because:
options: the mirror is smooth, so rays stay in order
the wall absorbs all the light
the wall does not reflect light
the mirror makes its own light
questions.answer: the mirror is smooth, so rays stay in order
questions.hint: Both surfaces reflect. Only one keeps the pattern.
questions.explanation: A rough wall scatters the rays in all directions, destroying the pattern. A mirror is smooth enough that the arrangement survives, so an image forms.

questions.question: A straw in a glass of water looks bent because:
options: light from it refracts at the water's surface
the straw really bends in water
questions.answer: light from it refracts at the water's surface
questions.hint: The straw is fine.
questions.explanation: Light from the submerged part bends as it leaves the water, so the brain - assuming a straight path - places that part somewhere it is not.

questions.question: A ray passes into a glass block without bending. That means it arrived:
questions.hint: What has to happen for one side of the beam to slow first?
questions.explanation: Arriving square to the surface, the whole beam enters at once, so nothing slows before anything else and there is nothing to pivot the ray.

questions.question: A shop window shows the street by day and your reflection at night because:
options: it always does both, and the brighter side wins
glass only reflects in the dark
questions.answer: it always does both, and the brighter side wins
questions.hint: Ask what actually changed between day and night.
questions.explanation: The glass reflects a little and transmits most at all times. By day the street is brighter, so you see through; at night the inside is brighter, so the reflection dominates.

units.unitOverview: Every human body changes as it grows from a child into an adult, and those changes are ordinary, expected and the same across the world. This unit names the parts of the human reproductive system and describes the physical changes of puberty, factually and without fuss, so that what happens to your body is something you understand rather than something that takes you by surprise.
sources: Cambridge Primary Science Teacher's Resource 6, topic on the human reproductive system and puberty
outcomes: Name the main parts of the male and female human reproductive systems.
State the job of each of those parts.
Explain what puberty is and roughly when it happens.
Describe the physical changes that happen to boys during puberty.
Describe the physical changes that happen to girls during puberty.
Recognise that the timing of these changes varies a great deal between people, and that this is normal.

concepts.title: The Parts, and What Each One Does
concepts.explanation:
You have studied several body systems: the circulatory system that moves blood, the respiratory system that takes in oxygen, the digestive system that processes food. The REPRODUCTIVE SYSTEM is another one, and it is the system by which humans produce children. Unlike the others it is not needed to keep a person alive, and it does not begin working until the body is much older.

There are two forms of it. In the MALE system: the TESTES are two organs held outside the body in a bag of skin called the scrotum, and their job is to make sperm cells; the PENIS is the organ through which sperm leave the body, and through which urine also leaves, by a tube called the urethra. Sperm are extremely small - far too small to see - and each one carries half the instructions needed to make a new person.

In the FEMALE system: the two OVARIES hold egg cells, and a female is born with all the eggs she will ever have; the OVIDUCTS, also called fallopian tubes, carry an egg from an ovary towards the uterus; the UTERUS, also called the womb, is a muscular organ where a baby grows if an egg is fertilised; the CERVIX is the narrow neck at the lower end of the uterus; and the VAGINA is the passage leading from the cervix to the outside of the body.

A new human begins when a sperm cell joins with an egg cell, which is called FERTILISATION - the same word and the same idea as in the flowering plants you studied earlier, where pollen joins with an ovule.

These are the correct scientific names, and knowing them matters for the same reason that knowing 'oesophagus' matters: you cannot ask a clear question, or understand a clear answer from a doctor or a nurse, without the right words.
concepts.example: The digestive system is a tube with a different job at each stage, and the reproductive system is built the same way: the testes make the cells, and a tube carries them out; the ovaries hold the cells, an oviduct carries one along, and the uterus is where a baby would grow. Naming the organ and naming its job is the same skill you used on the gut.

concepts.title: What Puberty Is
concepts.explanation:
PUBERTY is the period during which a child's body changes into an adult's body, and the reproductive system starts to work. It is not an illness and not an event - it is a stretch of several years during which a long list of changes happens gradually.

It is driven by HORMONES, which are chemical messengers made in the body and carried in the blood. At a certain age the brain begins signalling for more of these hormones to be produced, and they are what cause every change in this unit. Nobody decides to begin puberty and nobody can hurry it or delay it.

It usually begins somewhere between about 8 and 14 years old, and typically a year or two earlier in girls than in boys. It then continues for several years, so someone who starts at 10 may still be changing at 16.

The SPREAD IS THE MOST IMPORTANT FACT IN THIS UNIT. Two people of exactly the same age can be at completely different stages, and neither is early or late in any way that matters - they are simply both normal. In any class of twelve-year-olds some will have started and some will not, and both groups are exactly where they should be. Comparing yourself with a friend tells you nothing except that people differ, which you already knew.

Some changes happen to everybody: growing much taller and quite quickly, growing hair under the arms and between the legs, sweating more, and often getting spots because the skin makes more oil. Feelings change too - moods can be stronger and less predictable for a while - and that is caused by the same hormones and is just as ordinary as growing taller.
concepts.example: Three friends turn twelve in the same month. One has grown 8 cm in a year and needs new shoes constantly; one has grown 2 cm and nothing else has changed yet; one started changing at ten and has nearly finished growing. All three are entirely normal, and in four years' time the differences between them will have almost disappeared.

concepts.title: The Changes in Boys
concepts.explanation:
In boys, puberty usually starts between about 10 and 15, and the changes are caused by hormones from the testes.

The body grows FASTER AND TALLER, in a spurt that can add several centimetres in a year, and the shoulders and chest broaden. MUSCLE develops more than before, which is why strength increases noticeably over a year or two.

HAIR grows in new places: under the arms, between the legs, on the legs and arms, and later on the face. Facial hair usually comes late in the sequence, and it starts fine and sparse rather than as a beard.

The VOICE gets deeper. The voice box grows larger and the vocal cords lengthen and thicken, so they vibrate more slowly - which is exactly the pitch idea you met with strings and air columns: a longer, thicker, looser vibrating thing gives a lower note. While it is growing the voice can jump unpredictably between high and low, which is temporary and stops once the growing is finished.

The TESTES and PENIS grow larger, and the testes begin producing sperm, which is the point at which the reproductive system has started working.

The SKIN makes more oil, so spots are common, and the SWEAT GLANDS become more active, which is why washing daily and more carefully matters more than it did before.

All of this happens over several years and in no fixed order, and the pace varies enormously between individuals.
concepts.example: A boy's voice cracking mid-sentence is not a fault and not permanent. His voice box is growing, so the vocal cords are changing length and thickness while he is still using them - and the pitch settles as soon as the growth finishes, exactly as a guitar string settles once you stop turning the peg.

concepts.title: The Changes in Girls
concepts.explanation:
In girls, puberty usually starts between about 8 and 13 - often a year or two before boys of the same age - and the changes are caused by hormones from the ovaries.

The body grows FASTER AND TALLER in a spurt, which for girls tends to come earlier in the sequence than it does for boys, and the hips broaden. BREASTS develop, usually beginning as a small firm swelling under the nipple and continuing over several years.

HAIR grows under the arms and between the legs, and on the legs.

MENSTRUATION begins, which is often called having periods. Each month an ovary releases an egg, and the lining of the uterus thickens ready to support a baby if that egg is fertilised. If it is not, the lining is not needed and is shed through the vagina over a few days, as a small amount of blood. This happens roughly once a month, and it is an ordinary, healthy process rather than an illness or an injury. The first periods are often irregular and settle into a pattern over a year or two. Anyone menstruating needs clean sanitary products and somewhere private to change them, and washing is important - which is a matter of practical hygiene, not of anything being unclean.

The SKIN makes more oil, so spots are common, and the SWEAT GLANDS become more active.

As with boys, all of this happens over years, in no fixed order, and the timing varies greatly between individuals. Someone who starts at nine and someone who starts at thirteen are both normal.
concepts.example: A girl's first period may come as much as two years after her breasts begin to develop, and the first few may be weeks or months apart before settling into a cycle. Neither the gap nor the irregularity is a problem - the body is starting a process it will run for decades, and it does not start it neatly.

explorations.title: Naming the Parts and Their Jobs
explorations.context: To learn the parts of the reproductive system in the same way you learned the digestive system - by organ and by job.
explorations.prompt: Make two labelled lists, one for the male system and one for the female. Beside each part write one short sentence saying what it does. Then check your lists against the concept.
explorations.answer: Male: testes make sperm; the penis is the passage out. Female: ovaries hold eggs, oviducts carry an egg towards the uterus, the uterus is where a baby grows, the cervix is its neck, the vagina is the passage to the outside.
explorations.hint: Write the job before you look it up, then correct it. Trying first and then checking fixes a name far better than copying does.
explorations.explanation: The Parts, and What Each One Does: naming the organ and stating its job is exactly the skill you used on the digestive system.

explorations.title: How Much Do People Differ?
explorations.context: To see for yourself how wide the normal range is, using data rather than impressions.
explorations.prompt: Cambridge gives the usual start of puberty as about 8 to 14 years. Draw a number line from 7 to 16 and shade that range. Then mark where a person starting at 9 and a person starting at 13 would sit, and write what the shaded width tells you.
explorations.answer: The shaded band is about six years wide, so two people of the same age can be several years apart in development and both be entirely normal. The width of the band IS the finding.
explorations.hint: Do not use anyone real, including yourself - this is about the range, not about individuals.
explorations.explanation: What Puberty Is: the spread is the most important fact here, and a number line makes it something you can see rather than something you are told.

explorations.title: Why a Voice Deepens
explorations.context: To connect a change in puberty to the physics of pitch you already know.
explorations.prompt: Stretch a rubber band and pluck it. Now use a longer, thicker band at lower tension and pluck that. Describe the difference in pitch, then explain how this relates to a voice deepening.
explorations.answer: The longer, thicker, looser band gives a lower note, because it vibrates more slowly. The voice box grows and the vocal cords lengthen and thicken, so they vibrate more slowly and the voice deepens.
explorations.hint: Change one thing at a time - length first, then thickness - or you cannot say which caused what.
explorations.explanation: The Changes in Boys: a deepening voice is the pitch rule from the sound work applied to a part of the body that is growing.

methods.title: Describing a System by Organ and Job
methods.example: To set out a body system clearly, as you did for digestion.
steps: List the parts in a sensible order - the order a cell would travel, where there is one.
Give each part its correct scientific name.
Write one sentence for each saying what it DOES.
Check no two of your sentences say the same thing.
Read the list back and make sure someone who had not studied it could follow.

methods.title: Reading a Range Rather Than an Average
methods.example: To interpret a figure like 'puberty usually begins between 8 and 14'.
steps: Write down the lower and upper figures.
Work out the width of the range by subtracting.
Ask what the width means for two people of the same age.
State clearly that anywhere inside the range is normal, not just the middle.
Avoid turning the range into an average - 'about 11' loses the whole point of it.

methods.title: Tracing a Change Back to Its Cause
methods.example: To explain a physical change during puberty rather than just listing it.
steps: Name the change precisely.
Name the organ or tissue that is actually changing.
Say what hormones triggered it, and where they came from.
If the change involves something you have studied elsewhere - pitch, muscle, skin - connect it to that.
Say roughly how long it takes, since almost nothing here happens quickly.

workedExamples.title: Which organ makes sperm?
workedExamples.prompt: Name the organ that produces sperm cells, and say where it is.
workedExamples.solution: The testes, two organs held outside the body in a bag of skin called the scrotum. Their job is to make sperm cells, each of which carries half the instructions needed to make a new person. They begin producing sperm during puberty.

workedExamples.title: The path of an egg
workedExamples.prompt: An egg is released from an ovary. Name the parts it passes through or reaches, in order, and say what each is for.
workedExamples.solution: It leaves the ovary, which held it, and travels along an oviduct, whose job is to carry it. The oviduct leads to the uterus, the muscular organ where a baby grows if the egg is fertilised. Below the uterus is the cervix, its narrow neck, and below that the vagina, the passage to the outside of the body.

workedExamples.title: Why two twelve-year-olds can look so different
workedExamples.prompt: Two classmates are both exactly twelve. One has grown very tall this year and one has not changed much. Explain.
workedExamples.solution: Puberty usually begins anywhere between about 8 and 14, a range six years wide, and it is triggered by hormones on the body's own timetable rather than by anything the person does. So two people of identical age can easily be three or four years apart in development, and both are completely normal. Within a few years the difference between them will have largely disappeared.

workedExamples.title: Explaining menstruation clearly
workedExamples.prompt: Explain what menstruation is and why it happens, in two or three sentences.
workedExamples.solution: Each month an ovary releases an egg, and the lining of the uterus thickens ready to support a baby if that egg is fertilised. If the egg is not fertilised the thickened lining is not needed, so it is shed through the vagina over a few days as a small amount of blood. It is a healthy monthly process, not an illness or an injury, and it repeats roughly every month for many years.

practice.prompt: Which organs make sperm cells?
practice.answer: The testes.
practice.hint: They are held outside the body, in the scrotum.

practice.prompt: Which organs hold egg cells?
practice.answer: The ovaries.
practice.hint: A female is born with all the eggs she will ever have.

practice.prompt: What is the uterus for?
practice.answer: It is the muscular organ where a baby grows if an egg is fertilised.
practice.hint: It is also called the womb.

practice.prompt: What is puberty?
practice.answer: The period of several years during which a child's body changes into an adult's and the reproductive system starts working.
practice.hint: It is a stretch of time, not a single event.

practice.prompt: What causes the changes of puberty?
practice.answer: Hormones - chemical messengers made in the body and carried in the blood.
practice.hint: Nobody decides to start, and nobody can hurry it.

practice.prompt: Name three changes that happen to both boys and girls.
practice.answer: Any three of: growing taller quickly, hair growing under the arms and between the legs, sweating more, oilier skin and spots, stronger or less predictable moods.
practice.hint: Several changes are not particular to either.

practice.prompt: Why does a boy's voice deepen?
practice.answer: The voice box grows larger and the vocal cords lengthen and thicken, so they vibrate more slowly - and slower vibration gives a lower pitch.
practice.hint: It is the same rule as a thicker, looser guitar string.

practice.prompt: What happens during menstruation?
practice.answer: The lining of the uterus, which had thickened ready for a fertilised egg, is shed through the vagina over a few days when no egg is fertilised.
practice.hint: It happens roughly once a month and is a healthy process.

practice.prompt: Two people are the same age and at very different stages of puberty. What can you conclude?
practice.answer: Nothing except that people differ. Puberty normally begins anywhere across a range about six years wide, so both are normal and neither is early or late in any way that matters.
practice.hint: The width of the normal range is the answer.

practice.prompt: What is fertilisation, and where have you met the word before?
practice.answer: The joining of a sperm cell with an egg cell, which is when a new human begins. The same word and the same idea appeared in flowering plants, where pollen joins with an ovule.
practice.hint: You studied it in the plant units.

activities.title: Two systems, labelled
activities.materials: Paper, a pencil, and the concepts in this unit.
steps: Draw a simple outline diagram of each reproductive system.
Label every part with its correct scientific name.
Beside each label, write one short sentence saying what that part does.
Check your work against the concept, and correct any job you got wrong rather than rubbing it out.

activities.title: The normal range on a number line
steps: Draw a number line from 7 to 16 years.
Shade the band from 8 to 14, which is the usual range for puberty beginning.
Mark two imaginary people, one starting at 9 and one at 13, and label both 'normal'.
Write one sentence explaining what the width of that band means for a class of twelve-year-olds.

activities.title: Questions worth asking
steps: Write down any three questions this unit left you with.
For each, use the correct scientific names from the unit's word list.
Mark which of your questions science can answer and which is really about how you feel.
Decide who would be the right person to ask each one - a parent, a teacher, a nurse or a doctor.

rules.text: The reproductive system is how humans produce children; unlike other systems it is not needed to stay alive.
Puberty is caused by hormones, and nobody chooses when it starts.
Puberty normally begins anywhere between about 8 and 14, and everywhere in that range is normal.
Fertilisation is a sperm cell joining an egg cell - the same idea as in flowering plants.

terms: The body system by which humans produce children.
The two male organs that make sperm cells.
The male sex cell, carrying half the instructions for a new person.
The male organ through which sperm and urine leave the body.
The two female organs that hold egg cells.
The female sex cell, carrying half the instructions for a new person.
The tube carrying an egg from an ovary towards the uterus.
The muscular organ, also called the womb, where a baby grows.
The narrow neck at the lower end of the uterus.
The passage from the cervix to the outside of the body.
The joining of a sperm cell with an egg cell.
The years during which a child's body changes into an adult's.
A chemical messenger made in the body and carried in the blood.
The monthly shedding of the uterus lining when no egg is fertilised.
commonMistakes: Puberty happens all at once.
It takes several years and the changes come gradually, in no fixed order. Someone who starts at ten may still be changing at sixteen.
Everyone changes at the same age.
The normal range is about six years wide. Two classmates of the same age can be years apart in development and both be entirely normal.
Menstruation is an illness or an injury.
It is an ordinary healthy process: the uterus lining, thickened ready for a fertilised egg, is shed when no egg is fertilised.
A cracking voice is something going wrong.
The voice box is growing, so the vocal cords are changing length while still being used. It settles once the growth is finished.
Spots mean your skin is dirty.
The skin is making more oil because of hormones. Washing helps, but the cause is inside the body and not a matter of cleanliness.

connections.text: This is the fourth system you have studied, and it is described the same way as the others: name the organ, then say what it does.
Fertilisation here is the same idea as in the plant units - two sex cells joining - which is why the word is the same.
A deepening voice is the pitch rule you already know: a longer, thicker vibrating cord gives a lower note.
Knowing the correct names is what lets you ask a nurse or a doctor a clear question and understand the answer.

realProblems.context: A twelve-year-old is worried because several classmates have grown much taller this year and they have not.
realProblems.prompt: What does the science say, and what would you tell them?
realProblems.answer: That puberty normally begins anywhere between about 8 and 14, a range six years wide, and it is set by hormones on the body's own timetable. Being at a different stage from a classmate of the same age is completely normal and says nothing at all about them. Within a few years the differences will have largely evened out.
realProblems.hint: The width of the normal range is the whole answer.
realProblems.errorFeedback: The normal range is about six years wide, so being at a different stage from classmates the same age is ordinary and evens out.

realProblems.context: Someone at a clinic is asked by a nurse where exactly a pain is, and does not know the names of the parts.
realProblems.prompt: Why does knowing the correct scientific names matter here?
realProblems.answer: Because a vague description can be misunderstood and a precise one cannot. Naming the organ lets the nurse ask the right follow-up questions and rule things out quickly, and it lets the patient understand the answer. It is the same reason knowing 'oesophagus' or 'small intestine' matters.
realProblems.hint: Think about how the conversation goes if neither person can name the part.
realProblems.errorFeedback: Correct names let a clear question be asked and a clear answer be understood - exactly as with the digestive system.

realProblems.context: A boy is embarrassed that his voice keeps jumping between high and low when he speaks in class.
realProblems.prompt: Explain what is happening physically, and why it will stop.
realProblems.answer: His voice box is growing and the vocal cords are lengthening and thickening. Longer, thicker cords vibrate more slowly and so give a lower pitch - but while they are still changing size the pitch is unpredictable, because the cords are not the same as they were last week. Once the growth finishes the pitch settles, exactly as a guitar string holds its note once you stop turning the peg.
realProblems.hint: Connect it to the pitch rule from the sound work.
realProblems.errorFeedback: The vocal cords are growing longer and thicker, so the pitch is unsettled until the growth finishes - then it steadies.

reasoningPrompts.prompt: Why is it a mistake to compare your own development with a classmate's of the same age?
keyIdeas: The normal range is about six years wide
Hormones set the timing, not the person
Both are normal, and the differences even out
reasoningPrompts.modelAnswer: Because age is a poor guide to what stage someone's body has reached. Puberty normally begins anywhere between about 8 and 14, which is a range six years wide, and the timing is set by hormones on the body's own schedule rather than by anything the person does. So two classmates of exactly the same age can be several years apart in development and both be completely normal, and within a few years those differences will have largely disappeared.

reasoningPrompts.prompt: Explain how a deepening voice connects to what you learned about pitch.
keyIdeas: Pitch depends on how fast something vibrates
Longer and thicker vibrates more slowly
The voice box grows during puberty
reasoningPrompts.modelAnswer: Pitch depends on how fast the source vibrates: fast gives a high note and slow gives a low one, and a longer, thicker, looser vibrating thing vibrates more slowly. During puberty the voice box grows larger and the vocal cords lengthen and thicken, so they vibrate more slowly than before and the voice sounds deeper. It is the same rule that makes the thick strings on a guitar the low ones.

reasoningPrompts.prompt: Why is it useful to describe the reproductive system the same way you described the digestive system?
keyIdeas: Name the organ, then state its job
It makes the system understandable rather than memorised
The correct names allow clear questions
reasoningPrompts.modelAnswer: Because the method works on any body system: name each part, then say what it does. Used on digestion it turned a list of words into a journey that made sense, and it does the same here - the testes make the cells, a tube carries them out; the ovaries hold the cells, an oviduct carries one along, the uterus is where a baby would grow. Having the correct names and the correct jobs is also what lets someone ask a doctor or a nurse a clear question and understand the answer.
